narrative: Congenital heart disease (CHD) screening of newborns by pulse oximetry (NCDIMH guidelines, page 148). Measure oxygen saturation (O2 sat) in the right hand and any foot of all newborns at 24-36 hours of age. Abnormal: O2 sat below 90% in the right hand or any foot; screening failed, consult a paediatric cardiologist. Normal: O2 sat 95% or more in the right hand or any foot and a difference of 3% or less between hand and foot; screening passed. Indefinite: O2 sat 90-94% in the right hand and any foot, or a difference of more than 3% between hand and foot; repeat the measurement in 1 hour. If the repeat is abnormal, screening failed; if normal, screening passed; if indefinite again, repeat once more in 1 hour; a second repeat that is abnormal or indefinite means screening failed, and normal means passed.

narrative: Approach to suspected congenital heart disease (CHD) (NCDIMH guidelines, page 149). Suspect CHD with blue colour since birth that worsens with crying, poor or intermittent feeding, sweating during feeding, crying or sleeping, precordial bulge, exercise intolerance, recurrent lower respiratory tract infections, recurrent heart failure, squatting, cyanotic spells or loss of consciousness, or chest pain, breathlessness and palpitations. If there is no central cyanosis or hypoxia, it is acyanotic CHD: do chest X-ray, ECG and echocardiography. If there is central cyanosis, consider cyanotic CHD, pulmonary disease and non-cardiac causes such as sepsis, and do a hyperoxia test (15 L oxygen, measure O2 sat). If saturation does not rise, it is cyanotic CHD: chest X-ray, ECG and echocardiography. If it rises, consider pulmonary disease or non-cardiac causes; the hyperoxia test is not definitive and does not completely exclude CHD.

text:
Diagram: Acyanotic and Cyanotic CHD flowchart (section: Approach to suspected congenital heart disease)
- Acyanotic CHD -> Pressure overload: Clinical manifestations depend on the severity of the obstruction; Volume Overload: Clinical manifestations depend on the severity of the of the left-to right shunt
- Pressure overload: Clinical manifestations depend on the severity of the obstruction -> Pulmonary stenosis; Aortic stenosis; Coarctation of the aorta
- Volume Overload: Clinical manifestations depend on the severity of the of the left-to right shunt -> ASD; VSD/AVSD; PDA/AOW
- Pulmonary stenosis -> If critical, ductal dependents! Presents in the first days of life in shock If non-critical: Tachypnea, poor weight gain, poor feeding, ejection murmur over the pulmonary area
- Aortic stenosis -> If critical, ductal dependents! Presents in the first days of life in shock If non-critical: Tachypnea, poor weight gain, poor feeding, ejection murmur over the pulmonary area
- Coarctation of the aorta -> If critical, ductal dependents! Presents in the first days of life in shock If non-critical: HTN on upper limbs, radial artery to femoral artery pulse delay, systolic mummer irradiating at the back
- ASD -> Asymptomatic, can present with recurrent chest infections and poor weight gain Physical findings: no respiratory distress, ejection murmur (most of the time absent) pulmonary area, fixed split of S2
- VSD/AVSD -> Symptoms appear first weeks of life: Diaphoresis, poor weight gain, poor feeding, tachypnea, and tachycardia Physical findings: chest retraction, holosystolic murmur at LLSB, hepatomegaly, Harrison sulcus
- PDA/AOW -> Symptoms appear first weeks of life: Diaphoresis, poor weight gain, poor feeding, tachypnea, and tachycardia Physical findings: Chest retraction, continuous murmur at the left infraclavicular area, hepatomegaly
- If critical, ductal dependents! Presents in the first days of life in shock If non-critical: Tachypnea, poor weight gain, poor feeding, ejection murmur over the pulmonary area -> 1. - Cyanotic CHD -> Decreased pulmonary blood flow; Increased pulmonary blood flow; Others
- Decreased pulmonary blood flow -> TOF; Tricuspid Valve Diseases; Pulmonary Valve Atresia
- Increased pulmonary blood flow -> TGA; Truncus Arteriosus; TAPVR
- Others -> - HLHS, interrupted aortic arch, complex CHD - Variable-associated cardiac anomalies. - Symptoms depending on the importance of the pulmonary. - If in HF, treat as indicated in the HF algorithm. - Pediatric cardiologist to decide the indication and timing of cardiac surgery.
- TOF -> Clinical features: - Depending on the severity of the RVOTO - Tet spells, squatting, poor weight gain - Cyanosis, SEM ULSB, no hepatomegaly Imaging: - Chest x-ray: normal heart size with a boot shape, oligemic lungs - EKG, RAD, RAE, RVH
- Tricuspid Valve Diseases -> Types: - Tricuspid atresia - Tricuspid stenosis - Ebstein anommal Management: A pediatric cardiologist to assess the associated anomalies and recommend the proper medical and surgical management
- Pulmonary Valve Atresia -> - Severe form of TOF. - Ductal dependent and /or with MAPCAS. - Early presentation, marked central cyanosis, single and loud S2, continuous murmur radiating to the back and axillae - Very challenging surgical management and poor outcome
- TGA -> - Often associated with other cardiac anomalies. - Early presentation, absent or mid respiratory distress disproportionate to the high levels of cyanosis, absent or systolic murmur Imaging: - Chest x-ray. “egg on a string” appearance - EKG: often normal Management: PGEI, balloon atrial septostomy, astial switch
- Truncus Arteriosus -> - Presentation in the first days of life, mild to moderate cyanosis, symptoms, and signs of heart failure - Chest x-rays: cardiomegaly, increased pulmonary vascular markings - Treat as indicated in the HF algorithm - Surgical repair before PAH irreversible
- TAPVR -> - Early presentation if obstructed TAPVR with severe respiratory distress, marked cyanosis and shock - If unobstructed, Right HF symptoms and signs, fixed split S2, SEM, ULSB, hepatomegaly - Treat as indicated in the HF algorithm - Surgical repair and when the patient is stable
- Clinical features: - Depending on the severity of the RVOTO - Tet spells, squatting, poor weight gain - Cyanosis, SEM ULSB, no hepatomegaly Imaging: - Chest x-ray: normal heart size with a boot shape, oligemic lungs - EKG, RAD, RAE, RVH -> Management: - Tet spells: Knee-chest position, administer oxygen, IV Fluids: 10-20mV/ kg NS, Propranolol 0.1mg/kg/ dose. Definitive Management: Pediatric cardiologist to decide on the indication and timing of cardiac surgery

narrative: Acyanotic and cyanotic congenital heart disease (CHD) types and management (NCDIMH guidelines, page 150). Acyanotic, pressure overload: pulmonary stenosis, aortic stenosis and coarctation of the aorta; if critical they are ductal dependent and present in shock in the first days of life; if non-critical, tachypnoea, poor weight gain and feeding, ejection murmur (coarctation: hypertension in the upper limbs, radial-femoral pulse delay). Acyanotic, volume overload (left-to-right shunts): atrial septal defect (ASD, often asymptomatic, fixed split S2), ventricular septal defect or atrioventricular septal defect (symptoms in first weeks: sweating, poor weight gain, tachypnoea, holosystolic murmur at left lower sternal border, hepatomegaly) and patent ductus arteriosus (continuous murmur at left infraclavicular area). All acyanotic CHD: nutritional support, prevent URTI and endocarditis, treat heart failure (furosemide 1-3 mg/kg/day, spironolactone 1-3 mg/kg/day, captopril with caution 0.3-0.5 mg/kg/day), and treat the lesion surgically or by catheter. Cyanotic CHD with decreased pulmonary blood flow: tetralogy of Fallot (tet spells, squatting, boot-shaped heart; tet spell: knee-chest position, oxygen, IV fluids 10-20 mL/kg, propranolol 0.1 mg/kg), tricuspid valve disease and pulmonary atresia. With increased flow: transposition of the great arteries (egg-on-a-string X-ray; prostaglandin E1, balloon atrial septostomy, arterial switch), truncus arteriosus and TAPVR. Others, such as hypoplastic left heart syndrome: paediatric cardiologist decides on surgery.

## **CHAPTER 4**

## DERMATOLOGY

### **Atopic Dermatitis AD (Eczema)**

Chronic, pruritic inflammatory skin condition that occurs most frequently in children but may also affect adults. It follows a relapsing course. AD is often associated with elevated serum immunoglobulin levels and a family history of Type 1 allergies such as Allergic Rhinitis and Asthma.

narrative: Eczema management summary (NCDIMH guidelines, page 155; the printed heading is "Summary of Patient Management"). Assess disease history, extent, severity and impact on quality of life; educate patient and carer about care, trigger avoidance, and recognising flares and infections. Mild eczema: follow the eczema management plan (daily bathing, moisturisers applied top to toe at least twice daily, trigger avoidance) and follow up within two weeks; if improved, support optimal care at home (consider community-based services); if not improved, assess for skin infection and treatment compliance. Moderate or severe eczema: assess for skin infections and compliance. If unwell or febrile, consider hospitalisation and/or IV antimicrobials. If well, start flare treatment (moisturiser at least four times daily, eczema baths, topical steroids, wet dressings and compresses, oral antimicrobials if appropriate) and follow up within one week; if improved, support care at home; if not improved, consider hospitalisation and/or IV antimicrobials.

text:
### **Systemic Agents in the Treatment of Psoriasis**

Choice of treatment is largely based on disease severity, the presence of comorbid conditions, such as psoriatic arthritis and treatment history (e.g. responsiveness to topical therapy, tolerability). Topical therapy is the standard treatment for mild to moderate disease. Systemic therapy is reserved for moderate to severe disease. See table below.

text:
## **Child-Pugh Staging**

| **Parameter** | **1 Point** | **2 Points** | **3 Points** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Total bilirubin (µmol/L) (mg/dL)** | <34 (<2) | 34–50 (2–3) | >50 (>3) |
| **Serum albumin (g/L)** | >35 | 28–35 | <28 |
| **Prothrombin time prolongation (sec) or INR** | <4 sec or INR <1.7 | 4–6 sec or INR 1.7–2.3 | >6 sec or INR >2.3 |

narrative: West Haven grading of hepatic encephalopathy (NCDIMH guidelines, page 165). Unimpaired: no signs or symptoms and normal psychometric tests. Grade 0-1 (minimal or covert hepatic encephalopathy): no overt symptoms to mild decrease in attention span or awareness, altered sleep rhythm, abnormal psychometric tests. Grade 2: obvious personality change, inappropriate behaviour, asterixis, dyspraxia, lethargy, objectively disoriented to time. Grade 3: somnolence, gross disorientation, bizarre behaviour, objectively disoriented to time and space. Grade 4: coma.

heading_path: Chapter 5: Gastroenterology and Hepatology > Gastroduodenal Ulcers (PUD) > Helicobacter Pylori Related Peptic Ulcer Disease > Pharmacological Treatment
text:
## **Pharmacological Treatment**

Triple therapy is indicated for complete eradication of the organism.

**Note:**
H.pylori diagnostic tests should be repeated 5 weeks after the last dose of eradication therapy, and the PPI should be stopped 2weeks before testing the H.pylori stool antigen test to confirm eradication.

## **Gastritis**

This is an inflammatory mucosal response to injury from variety of agents and mechanisms including infections, drugs, alcohol, acute stress, radiation, allergy, acid and bile, ischemia or direct trauma. The inflammation may involve the entire stomach (pangastritis) or a region of the stomach (antral gastritis) while the severity of inflammation may be erosive or non-erosive.

## **Differential diagnosis of UGIB**

| **Presentation** | **Diagnosis** |
| --- | --- |
| Dyspepsia, H. pylori infection, NSAID use, anticoagulation, severe medical illness | Peptic ulcer disease |
| Stigmata of chronic liver disease, evidence of portal hypertension or risk factors for cirrhosis (alcohol use, viral hepatitis) | Variceal bleeding |
| History of heavy alcohol use and retching before hematemesis, hematemesis following weightlifting, or young adult with bulimia | Mallory-Weiss tear |
| Heartburn, regurgitation, and dysphagia; usually small-volume or occult bleeding | Esophagitis |
| Progressive dysphagia, weight loss, early satiety, or abdominal pain; usually small-volume or occult bleeding | Oesophageal or gastric cancer |
| NSAID use, heavy alcohol intake, severe medical illness; usually small-volume or occult bleeding | Gastroduodenal erosions |

• Commonly caused by UV light or very short flash or flame exposure
• Skin is red, dry & hypersensitive
• No treatment except analgesia
• Leaves no scarring on healing | | --- | --- | | **2nd Degree Burns** | **Superficial.**
• Epidermis + **Upper bl** of Dermis
• Commonly caused by scald (spill or splash)
• **Red, moist, weeping**, cob blisters that **blanche** with pressure
• Painful - due to nerve exposure, & heals from 7-14 days
• Leaves no scarring on healing but there is potential pigmentary changes | | | **Deep.**
• Epidermis + Upper a of Dermis
• Commonly caused by scald, flame, chemicals, oil & grease
• **Cheesy white, wet or waxy dry; Do not blanch**e with pressure
• Healing takes > 21days
• Severe scarring & risk of contractures | | **3rd Degree Burns (Full Thickness Burns)** | • Full Epidermis + Dermis are destroyed leaving no cells to heal
• Commonly caused by scald, steam, flame, chemicals, oil, grease & high voltage electricity
• Grey to charred & black, **insensate**, contracted, pale, leathery tissue
• Severe scarring & high risk of contractures | | ***4th Degree Burns*** | • Muscle involvement | | **5th Degree Burns** | • Bone involvement - Especially in epileptics who convulse during burning |

text: **Do not include first degree burns in the calculation of % TBSA.** The surface area of a **patient’s palm (including fingers)** is roughly **1% of TBSA**. Palmar surface can be used to estimate relatively small burns (< **15%** of total surface area) or very large burns (> 85%, when unburnt skin is counted). For **medium-sized burns**, it is **inaccurate**.

text:
| **Stage** | **Key Actions** | | --- | --- | | **First Aid
(Immediate Care)** | - Drench burn with cool water to prevent further damage
- Remove burned clothing if easily removable
- If burn area is limited → immerse in cold water for 30 min (reduces pain, oedema, tissue damage)
- If burn area is large → cover with clean wraps to prevent hypothermia
- Beware of Hypothermia risk: especially in young children
- Critical window: first 6 hours → transport severe burn cases to hospital urgently | | **Initial Wound Care** | - Administer tetanus prophylaxis in all cases if possible
- Debride bullae (except very small burns) C excise necrotic tissue (continue over first few days)
- Gentle scrubbing to remove loose tissue
- Cleansing: use 0.25% chlorhexidine, 0.1% cetrimide, or other mild antiseptic (avoid alcohol-based solutions)
- Apply thin layer of antibiotic cream (silver sulfadiazine)
- Dress with petroleum gauze + dry gauze thick enough to prevent seepage | | **Daily Wound Care** | - Change dressing daily (twice daily if seepage)
- Remove loose tissue during each change
- Inspect wounds for discoloration or haemorrhage (infection signs)
- Systemic antibiotics: for haemolytic streptococcal infection or septicaemia
- Pseudomonas infection → treat with systemic aminoglycosides
- Topical agents:- Silver nitrate 0.5%: cheap, occlusive dressings, no eschar penetration, causes electrolyte loss C stains |

narrative: Snakebite management by venom type (NCDIMH guidelines, page 182). Syndromes: mixed cytotoxic and neurotoxic (rinkhals, berg adder, garter snakes, shield-nose snake); cytotoxic (puff adders, Gaboon vipers, spitting cobras, stiletto snakes, night adders, horned adders); neurotoxic (black and green mamba, non-spitting cobras); haemotoxic (boomslang, vine snake). Supportive care: IV fluids, analgesia with paracetamol (not aspirin or NSAIDs), protect the airway, elevate the limb; for haemotoxic bites give blood components (heparin and antifibrinolytics are of no value and maybe dangerous). Anticipate severe envenomation with drowsiness, vomiting, weakness; swelling over 5 cm/hour, to elbow or knee within 6 hours, or whole limb in 12 hours, or bleeding abnormalities; metallic taste, sweating, salivation, ptosis, fasciculation, breathlessness; or persistent fang-puncture bleeding, headaches, convulsions (20-minute clot test). Antivenom: IV line in another limb, pre-dose adrenaline 0.25 mg subcutaneously, doctor administers, no test dose. Polyvalent for rinkhals, puff adder, spitting cobras and Gaboon adder (vials added to 200 mL saline over 30 minutes), polyvalent plus atropine and neostigmine for cobras, monovalent for boomslang and vine snake. Starting doses: rinkhals 50 mL; puff adder 50-100 mL; Mozambique spitting cobra 100 mL+; Gaboon adder 200 mL; black mamba or snouted cobra 80-200 mL; boomslang or vine snake 20 mL. Give more if swelling continues, neurological signs do not improve in 30 minutes (4 vials), or blood stays incoagulable at 6 hours. Monitor for anaphylaxis.

text:
(Adapted for the South African Snakebite Symposium 2022)
(Snake Management South African Consensus Guideline - SAA 2022)
(Swaziland Antivenom Foundation 2018)
ISO ED 00107 V1 Nov 2019 NETCARE

(Blaylock, 2005) and see also Muller et al SAMJ 2012 - use of atropine and neostigmine

**Administration of Antivenom:**
* **Give the first dose (10ml) of antivenom intravenously at the slow rate of 1-2 ml per minute. Subsequent doses may be injected into a bag of saline drip, no more than 20 ml per 500ml bag to run in 30 mins. Repeat until symptoms are resolved. Monitor breathing and other vital signs continuously. Remember not to have the drip running direct into the wounded limb which is already in danger from the pressure of swelling and should be kept elevated and well protected.**
* **Remember to have adrenaline (1:1,000) at the bedside in case of anaphylaxis. If the patient has known allergies (asthma etc.), draw up the adrenaline (0.3 - 0.5 ml for adults and 0.1 - 0.3 for children) and have antihistamine available in case allergic symptoms are overwhelming. Antihistamine is NOT recommended as routine treatment for snakebite.**
* **Monitor breathing and other vital signs continuously.**
* **DO NOT infiltrate the bite area with antivenom.**

text:
### **In-Hospital Management of Traumatic Brain Injury**

| ICP control measures: On going care | ICP control measures: On going care |
| --- | --- |
| Elevate Head of bed | 30-40 degrees (adult and child) |
| Hyperosmolar Agents | Hypertonic saline or Mannitol |
| Control Blood Pressure | Hypertensive crisis (Treat with IV Labetalol or Nicardipine) |
| Control Blood Pressure | Avoid Hypotension (IVF and vasopressors) |
| Control Blood Sugar | 6-8 mmol/L |
| Thromboembolism Prophylaxis | Enoxaparin (LMWH), compression stockings |
| Others | Enteral nutrition with target 25 - 30kcal/kg/day by day 7, Keep Hb > 7g/dL |
| Severe TBI (GCS<8) |  |
| Airway management | GCS<8: Intubation and admit to ICU |
| Ventilation | PaCO2 32-37mmHg |
| Sedation for 48-72 hours | Midazolam OR Propofol plus Morphine |
| Prophylactic AED | Phenytoin |
| Start on empiric antibiotic | Risk of nosocomial infection and meningitis |
| Stress Ulcer Prophylaxis | Proton pump inhibitors, H2 receptor blockers or sucralfate |

text:
## Acute Kidney Injury Causes | Kidney Region | Cause of Acute Kidney Injury | | --- | --- | | **Pre-Renal** | *Dehydration* - Kucatseka, diarrhoea, vomiting, sweating
*Shock* - Cardiogenic, septic, haemorrhagic
***Drugs*** - BP Theraphy, Non steroidal anti inflammatory drug (NSAIDS) | | **Intrinsic Renal** | *Tubules* - acute tubular necrosis ( from ischaemia from untreated pre-renal causes, sepsis toxins like myoglobin in rhabdomyolysis, light chains in mye loma, radio-iodine contrast, drugs such as aminoglycosides, rifampicine, amphotericin B, tenofovir, traditional remedies, some Chinese medicines) OR tubulitis
*Interstitium* - acute interstitial nephristitial nephritis (from drug eg rifampicin, bactrim) and from sepsis, autoimmune
*Glomeruli* - glomerulonephritis eg post infection/ autoimmune - can be drug unduced
*Vessels* - vasculitis, malignant hypertension, scleroderma, renal artery stenosis, pre-eclampsia | | **Post Renal** | *Urinary tract obstruction* - cancer of the cervix, rectum, or prostate (also begin prostatic enlargement), renal stones, iatrogenic ureteric laceration, retroperitoneal fibrosis, intra-tubular crystals (eg acyclovir) |

narrative: Diagnosis and management of acute kidney injury (AKI) (NCDIMH guidelines, page 202). Take a history (fluid intake and losses, oedema, severe illness, poor or no urine output for more than 6 hours) and examine (tachycardia, JVP, oedema, dry mucosa, weak pulses, reduced consciousness). Investigate: renal function, electrolytes, urine sediment, abdominal ultrasound, ECG if potassium is high. Stage AKI (KDIGO/AKIN): stage 1 creatinine 1.5 times baseline or urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/hour for 6 hours; stage 2 creatinine 2 times baseline or urine output below 0.5 for 12 hours; stage 3 creatinine above 3 times baseline (or above 356) or urine output below 0.5 for 24 hours. Stage 3: refer to a paediatric nephrologist at a centre that can do renal replacement therapy (RRT); stable stage 3 referrals are discussed with a physician and the receiving facility first. Stage 1 or 2: assess volume status. Hypovolaemia is pre-renal (dehydration, GI losses, third spacing, blood loss, reduced cardiac output, sepsis, hepatorenal syndrome): CBC, LFTs, CXR, ECG, echo. Euvolaemia is intrinsic renal (renal artery stenosis, vasculitis, HUS, glomerulonephritis, interstitial nephritis, acute tubular necrosis from nephrotoxic drugs, rhabdomyolysis, contrast): serum, urine eosinophils, renal ultrasound with Doppler. The third branch is also pre-renal or post-renal obstruction (posterior urethral valves, stones, clot, tumours, retroperitoneal fibrosis): imaging, urologist and nephrologist consult, relieve obstruction. Treat the cause, avoid nephrotoxic drugs, monitor weight, urine output, urea and electrolytes, creatinine, bicarbonate, calcium, phosphate and FBC daily.

Clinical Guidelines for the Management of Common NCDs, Injuries and Mental Health Conditions (NCDIMH) | Chapter 7: Nephrology > Diagnosis of Acute Kidney Injury > Algorithm for Diagnosis and Management of Acute Kidney Injury (page 202)

Diagnosis and management of acute kidney injury (AKI) (NCDIMH guidelines, page 202). Take a history (fluid intake and losses, oedema, severe illness, poor or no urine output for more than 6 hours) and examine (tachycardia, JVP, oedema, dry mucosa, weak pulses, reduced consciousness). Investigate: renal function, electrolytes, urine sediment, abdominal ultrasound, ECG if potassium is high. Stage AKI (KDIGO/AKIN): stage 1 creatinine 1.5 times baseline or urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/hour for 6 hours; stage 2 creatinine 2 times baseline or urine output below 0.5 for 12 hours; stage 3 creatinine above 3 times baseline (or above 356) or urine output below 0.5 for 24 hours. Stage 3: refer to a paediatric nephrologist at a centre that can do renal replacement therapy (RRT); stable stage 3 referrals are discussed with a physician and the receiving facility first. Stage 1 or 2: assess volume status. Hypovolaemia is pre-renal (dehydration, GI losses, third spacing, blood loss, reduced cardiac output, sepsis, hepatorenal syndrome): CBC, LFTs, CXR, ECG, echo. Euvolaemia is intrinsic renal (renal artery stenosis, vasculitis, HUS, glomerulonephritis, interstitial nephritis, acute tubular necrosis from nephrotoxic drugs, rhabdomyolysis, contrast): serum, urine eosinophils, renal ultrasound with Doppler. The third branch is also pre-renal or post-renal obstruction (posterior urethral valves, stones, clot, tumours, retroperitoneal fibrosis): imaging, urologist and nephrologist consult, relieve obstruction. Treat the cause, avoid nephrotoxic drugs, monitor weight, urine output, urea and electrolytes, creatinine, bicarbonate, calcium, phosphate and FBC daily.

narrative: Acute kidney injury (AKI) management: fluids, hypertension, electrolytes, nutrition and dialysis (NCDIMH guidelines, page 203). Fluid management by volume status: hypovolaemia, NaCl 0.9% bolus 20 mL/kg then rehydration; euvolaemia, insensible losses (400 mL/m2 or 30 mL/kg/day) plus urine and GI losses; hypervolaemia, insensible losses and furosemide 2-4 mg/kg (in nephrotic syndrome consider 25% albumin 0.5-1 g/kg over 30-60 minutes then a diuretic). Hypertension: furosemide IV 1-2 mg/kg/dose if fluid overloaded (second dose 6 hours later, maximum 6 mg/kg), amlodipine 0.05-0.3 mg/kg once daily (maximum 10 mg), IV labetalol 0.2-1 mg/kg/dose if severe; avoid ACE inhibitors and ARBs in AKI. Hyperkalaemia: 10% calcium gluconate 0.5-1 mL/kg over 10 minutes, glucose with insulin 0.1 IU/kg, salbutamol nebuliser, sodium bicarbonate, calcium resonium (kayexalate) 1 g/kg. Hyponatraemia below 118 mmol/L: calculate the deficit and give 3% saline to target 125. Hypocalcaemia: 10% calcium gluconate. Acidosis: 8.4% sodium bicarbonate by deficit, or 1-2 mmol/kg/dose three times daily. Nutrition: 95-115 kcal/kg, introduce protein gradually from day 2. Urgent dialysis and referral to tertiary renal replacement therapy (RRT) for: hyperkalaemia (threshold printed as above 605 mmol/L) unresponsive to treatment; fluid overload with pulmonary oedema resistant to furosemide; urea above 40 mmol/L (30 in neonates); sodium below 120 or above 160; pH below 7.2 that cannot be corrected; multi-system failure; anticipated prolonged oliguria. Discuss urgent RRT referrals with a physician and the receiving facility first.

| AKI | Oliguria |  |

| AKD | Decrease in GFR by > 35% or increase in SCr by > 50% for < 3 mo | Kidney damage > 3 mo |
| NKD | GFR > 60ml/min per 1.73 m² | No damage |
| NKD | Stable SCr without AKI/AKD/CKD |  |

Stage 1 AKI of short duration (1 day), creatinine back to baseline, healthy patient: consider the KAMPS bundle within 1 year. Stage 1 AKI lasting 1-2 days, limited comorbidities, no prior CKD, creatinine not back to baseline: consider KAMPS in 6 months. Prolonged stage 1 (3-6 days) or stage 2 of shorter duration (1-3 days), increasing comorbidities, persistently elevated creatinine: labs in 3-6 weeks and a long-term KAMPS or nephrology appointment within several months. Prolonged stage 2 (more than 7 days) with injury on urinalysis, multiple comorbidities (cancer, prior AKI, mild CKD), creatinine persistently elevated above 25% of baseline. Prolonged stage 3 and other persistent kidney disease with prior AKI, significant cardiovascular disease, hypertension, diabetes or advanced CKD: labs within days of discharge and nephrology or KAMPS appointment within a week. Stage 3 AKI, recovered or not, prior CKD stage 4, or recurrent AKI/AKD: KAMPS or WATCH ME labs within days of discharge and nephrology follow-up within 1 week.

heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Pharmacological Management of acute Kidney Injury Management > Fluid Challenge/Inotropes
text:
## Fluid Challenge/Inotropes | Adults | Children | | --- | --- | | Fluid bolus of 500ml isotonic fluid (preferably Ringer Lactate) over 15 minutes and reassess progress (BP, pulse, JVP, urine output) up to a total of 2 litres to achieve mean arterial pressure >65mmHg.
Start inotropes if adequate fluid challenge but still hypotensive to avoid fluid overload and to ensure tissue perfusion e.g Adrenaline 4mg(4amps) in 200 mls of N/S IV at 10ml/hr
**REMEMBER** to look for hypoglycaemia/sepsis/ other associated complications and start treatment as indicated Request Intensive Care Unit review urgently | Rehydrate per protocol for age and body weight
**If mild dehydration.** give oral rehydration solution at 5ml or 1 teaspoon every 5 minutes to replace losses OR 10ml/kg body weight for each loose stool;
**If moderate dehydration** give 5ml oral rehydration solution every 5 minutes to total 50-100ml/kg body weight over 2-4 hours
**If severe dehydration** and failed oral rehydration solution start cautious rehydration – give a bolus of 20ml/kg isotonic fluid such as Ringer Lactate intravenously. Followed by maintenance intravenous fluids per paediatric protocols.
URGENT REFERRAL FOR ICU CARE. DO NOT OVERHYDRATE AS LINKED TO INCREASED MORTALITY |

## **Clinical contexts for fluid administration in patients with or at risk of AKI** | **Clinical context** | **Reasons for fluid administration and** **potential benefits** | **Challenges and risks of fluid administration** | | --- | --- | --- | | **Age and demographics**

Children

Adults | • Diseases with volume losses

• Indications likely to be context-dependent | • Narrow window between hypovolemia and fluid overload
• Clear adverse effects of fluid overload
• Adverse effects of “one size fits all” approach to fluid management
• Uncertain definition of clinically significant fluid overload
• In patients with heart disease, poor cardiac reserve to tolerate hypovolemia and hypervolemia
• In patients with diastolic dysfunction, risk of potentiating venous hypertension and renal congestion in fluid overload | | **Settings**

Resource-limited

Pre-hospital Ward/ICU | • Specific condition including diarrheal illness

• Impetus toward early resuscitation

• Dynamic phases of illness associated with hypovolemia | • Differing spectrum of disease
• Potentially delayed presentation to secondary care
• Limited range of therapeutic options
• Lack of advanced hemodynamic monitoring
• Inappropriate administration of maintenance fluid
• Risk of “fluid-creep” leading to insidious fluid overload |

text:
## Complications of Acute Kidney Injury | Short Term | Long Term | | --- | --- | | 1. Fluid overload related – pulmonary edema, hypertension
2. Electrolyte related – hyperkalemia with risks of bradycardia and asystole or ventricular fibrillation
3. Metabolic acidosis – Kussmaul respiration
4. Uraemic – uraemic pericarditis (risk of tamponade especially following haemorrhagic conversion from heparin use during haemodialysis); uraemic encephalopathy (tremor, confusion, coma, seizures)
5. Electrolyte related – may have hypocalcaemia (seizures, tetany – though commoner in CKD)
6. Systemic toxicity from accumulation of renally cleared pharmacologic agents – e.g. Gadolinium, ethambutol | 1. Progression to CKD
2. Worsening of underlying CKD
3. Mortality risk
4. Cardiovascular risk |

text:
### **Causes of Pregnancy-Related Acute Kidney Injury**

image: timeline of causes of PR-AKI across pregnancy trimesters and postpartum period

#### **Disease-specific Treatment of Acute Kidney Injury in Pregnancy**

| **Causes of AKI during pregnancy** | **Treatment** |
| --- | --- |
| Hyperemesis gravidarum/prerenal causes | Hydration |
| Septic abortion/urinary tract infection | Antibiotics |
| Preeclampsia/HELLP/acute fatty liver of pregnancy | Delivery |
| Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura | Plasma exchange, rituximab |
| Atypical hemolytic syndrome | Eculizumab |
| Obstructive uropathy | Analgesics, stent, nephrostomy |

narrative: Screening algorithm for kidney disease (NCDIMH guidelines, page 213). Area population with risk factors (high blood pressure, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, family history of CKD): screen with blood glucose, spot urine, blood pressure and family history, and measure kidney function (serum creatinine or cystatin C, eGFR) and kidney injury (albuminuria or proteinuria). Population with no markers of risk: do not screen. CKD is present if eGFR is below 60 mL/min/1.73 m2, or there is albuminuria or proteinuria (ACR above 30 mg/mmol). If yes: lifestyle modification (stop smoking, balanced diet, exercise, sodium below 2 g/day), medical treatment (control blood pressure, diabetes and lipids; ACEi/ARB, SGLT2 inhibitors, metformin, statins), considerations (drug dosing, contrast media, hyperkalaemia, anaemia, bone disease, heart failure, hepatitis C, metabolic acidosis), then retesting, follow-up and nephrology referral when appropriate. If no: rescreen based on future patient assessment.

text:
**Algorithm to screen, risk stratify and treat chronic kidney disease (CKD).** Based on Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) guidelines and adapted from Vassalotti et al. 54,55 Care for older adults or those with limited life expectancy, including necessity of screening for CKD and treatment recommendations, should be individualized based on clinical status and patient preference. If estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) cr 45-49 ml/min per 1.73 m2 or in individuals with low muscle mass, chronic illness, malnutrition, or other circumstances, order cystatin C to estimate glomerular filtration rate (GFR). There are no current evidence-based recommendations regarding frequency of screening. Consider using risk equations, 9e.g., from CKD Prognosis Consortium) to estimate interval risk of developing CKD. Cause of CKD is classified based on clinical evaluation. Based on level 2 recommendation, which means most people would adopt systolic blood pressure target < 120 mm Hg while many others may opt for less-intensive approach. As there is likely to be marked variability in how individual patients weigh and value the potential benefits and harms of intensive blood pressure (BP) control (continued)

narrative: CKD risk, classification and management algorithm (NCDIMH guidelines, page 215). Conditions of CKD risk: hypertension, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, AKI or hospitalisation history, family history of kidney disease, obesity, older age, other risks. Screen with urine albumin-creatinine ratio (ACR) and serum creatinine and cystatin C to estimate eGFR. CKD is present if for 3 months or more: eGFR below 60, ACR above 30 mg/g (3 mg/mmol), or other markers of kidney disease; otherwise periodically repeat evaluation. Then classify by eGFR category (G1 90 or more, G2 60-89, G3b 30-44, G4 15-29, G5 below 15) and albuminuria category (A1 below 30 mg/g, A2 30-300, A3 above 300). Patient safety if eGFR below 60: dose drugs by eGFR, avoid AKI from volume depletion, sick-day rules, no dual ACEi/ARB, contrast precautions; eGFR 45-59 avoid prolonged NSAIDs; 30-44 also metformin at 50% dose; below 30 avoid NSAIDs, bisphosphonates and metformin, and monitor INR on warfarin. Slowing progression: ACEi/ARB if ACR above 30 mg/g, sodium below 2000 mg/day, HbA1c target 6.5-8.0% with metformin and SGLT2 inhibitor then GLP1-RA; test for anaemia, acidosis (bicarbonate below 22), bone disease; vaccinations; screen for hepatitis C. Reduce cardiovascular risk: systolic target below 120 mmHg, statin if CKD and age 50 or over, aspirin for secondary prevention. Refer to nephrology for AKI, eGFR below 30, ACR above 300 mg/g, progression, red cell casts, resistant hypertension, potassium abnormalities, nephrolithiasis or hereditary disease.

## Patient Assessment

### **Clinical Signs of CKD – always look for clues to the underlying cause**

* **CKD G1,2:** early - asymptomatic, normal acid-base and fluid balance - due to adaptive increase in function in the remaining nephrons
* **CKD G3a-b:** usually asymptomatic, low erythropoietin, low calcitriol, secondary hyperparathyroidism
* **CKD G4:** pallor (anaemia), metabolic acidosis, hypocalcaemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperkalaemia
* **CKD G5:** uremic fetor, uremic pericarditis, fluid overload, hypertension, anorexia, nausea, dyspepsia, pruritus, may or may not have oliguria

text:
**Interventions to slow chronic kidney disease (CKD) progression and/or reduce cardiovascular risk.**
<sup>a</sup>Unclear if and when to discontinue renin-angiotensin system (RAS) inhabitation in advanced CKD. <sup>b</sup>stains should be initiated for those beginning dialysis therapy. However, patients already receiving statins at the same time of dialysis initiation can continue their satin treatment. <sup>c</sup>Applies to CKD patients with type 2 diabetes only. SGLT2 inhibitor is recommended as first-line treatment with metformin and may also have benefits in persons with CKD and no diabetes.<sup>67,68</sup> Sodium-glucose contrasporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors should be initiated if estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) 30 ml and can be continued through G4-G5 until dialysis initiation, at which point SGLT2 inhibitor should be discontinued. There is no evidence for initiation of SGLT 2inhibitors if eGFR<30ml/min per 1.73m<sup>2</sup>. <sup>d</sup>Applies to CKD patients with type 2 diabetes only. Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist can be considered when SGLT2 inhibitor and/or metformin is not tolerated or by glycemic target is not reached. Dulaglutide can be used if eGFR > 15ml/min per 1.73m<sup>2</sup>; exenatide can be used if creatinine clearance > 30ml/min; there are limited data for use of liraglutide, lixisenatide, or semaglutide in severe CKD. Consult dosing recommendations for use of these agents in CKD G4 and GS.

text:
## **Principles of Chronic Kidney Disease Management**

| Category | All Stages (CKD 1–5) | Stage 1–3/4 | Stage 4–5 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Goals | Early detection, slow progression, prevent AKI, manage CV risk, adjust meds, immunize | Delay progression, prevent acute on chronic events, manage comorbidities | Prepare for RRT, manage complications |
| Screening | Screen high-risk populations (e.g., DM, HTN, elderly) | Regular renal function tests, proteinuria assessment | As in stage 1–3, plus closer nephrology follow-up |
| Risk Factor Control | Control BP, glucose, avoid nephrotoxins, lifestyle interventions | Use ACEi/ARB if proteinuria Lifestyle: diet, exercise, smoking cessation | Continue risk factor management, stricter control |
| Cardiovascular Care | Treat dyslipidaemia, hypertension, diabetes | Initiate statins if indicated | Intensify CV risk monitoring and treatment |
| Medication Management | Annual influenza, 5-year pneumococcal, Hepatitis B if seronegative | Same as all stages | Same as all stages |
| Medication Management | Review all meds for renal dosing | Monitor for dose accumulation | Dose adjustment critical due to declining GFR |
| Preventing AKI | Educate on avoiding dehydration, NSAIDs, and nephrotoxic agents | Monitor during infections or surgeries | Same, with increased vulnerability |
| Preparation for RRT | — | — | Educate on RRT options (HD, PD, transplant), plan access |

## (k) **CKD in Paediatric Population**

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| (1) Kidney damage for ≥3 months, as evidenced by structural or functional abnormalities of the kidney, with or without decreased GFR, manifested by 1 or more of the following features: - Abnormalities in the composition of the blood or urine - Abnormalities in imaging tests - Abnormalities on kidney biopsy (2) GFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² for ≥3 mo., with or without the other signs of kidney damage described above | - It is crucial to recognize children in the early stages of CKD for optimal evaluation and care. - Monitoring a child with CKD regularly provides an opportunity to control factors that can aggravate the progression of CKD. - The main treatable causes of CKD in children in developing countries are Urinary tract abnormalities, Acute kidney injury, and nephrotic syndrome. - The management of these diseases will be discussed separately |
| The cause should be identified for planning management strategies and prognosis. - Major causes of CKD in children are Congenital abnormalities of the kidney and urinary tract, reflux nephropathy, inherited disorders, glomerular diseases, renal stone, secondary to AKI, and Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome / thrombotic microangiopathy. |  |

narrative: Classification of glomerulonephritis (NCDIMH guidelines, page 224). Non-proliferative: minimal change (abnormal podocytes on electron microscopy; supportive care plus prednisolone, most respond well); membranous (thickened basement membrane, usually idiopathic; one third chronic, one third remit, one third progress to renal failure); focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (nephrotic syndrome, steroids often ineffective, 50% progress to renal failure). Proliferative: IgA nephropathy (most common in adults, macroscopic haematuria 24-48 hours after upper respiratory or GI infection); rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis, which includes vasculitic disorders: Goodpasture syndrome (anti-GBM antibody, glomerulus and lung, haematuria and haemoptysis; steroids), Wegener granulomatosis (c-ANCA positive; steroids plus cyclophosphamide), microscopic polyangiitis (p-ANCA positive; long-term steroids with or without cytotoxic agents); membranoproliferative (primary immune-mediated or secondary to SLE or hepatitis, usually progresses to end-stage renal failure); post-infectious (weeks after URTI, usually Streptococcus pyogenes, supportive treatment, resolves in 2-4 weeks).

• Complement studies (C3, C4)
• Serum lipids
• Serum electrolytes
• Confirm the presence of nephrotic syndrome (albumin, cholesterol, urine dipstick & spot urine protein/creatinine ratio)
• Exclude an underlying systemic or exogenous cause of nephrotic syndrome, that may require treatment (diabetes, HIV, VDRL, Hep B, Lupus serology, ANA and anti-ds DNA antibody etc., underlying malignancy e.g. myeloma causing amyloidosis)
• Determine renal function (creatinine, GFR – note may be falsely low because of low muscle mass)
• Exclude complications of nephrotic syndrome (sepsis from urinary losses of immunoglobulins – e.g. ascitic tap, doppler studies to exclude venous thrombosis)
• Determine the need for a kidney biopsy (e.g. in children deteriorating kidney function, refractory proteinuria) | 1. **Primary Nephrotic Syndromes**
• Minimal Change Disease (MCD)
• Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)
• Membranous Nephropathy
• Membranoproliferative Glomerulonephritis (MPGN)
2. **Secondary Causes**
• Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)
• Diabetes Mellitus (Diabetic nephropathy)
• Amyloidosis
• Infections: such as HIV and hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and Syphilis.
• Drug-Induced Nephropathy |

text:
## **Management of Acute Glomerulonephritis**

1. Low salt diet
2. Adequate but not excess protein diet
3. Ideally immunise before starting immunosuppressive therapy (pneumococcal vaccine to be repeated every 5 years, hepatitis B)
4. Screen for infections before commencing immunosuppressive therapy
5. Low sugar diet for those on glucocorticoids and calcineurin inhibitors

narrative: Glomerulonephritis and nephrotic syndrome pharmacological management (NCDIMH guidelines, page 227). The printed flowchart is partly garbled. Initial treatment: intense daily prednisone 60 mg/m2 (2 mg/kg); if remission within 4 weeks, consolidation with alternate-day prednisone for 8 weeks (40 mg/m2 every 48 hours for 4 weeks, then 20 mg/m2 every 48 hours for 4 weeks), then stop. Relapsing idiopathic nephrotic syndrome: infrequent relapses, prednisone 60 mg/m2 daily until remission then 40 mg/m2 alternate days for 4 weeks. Frequent relapses or glucocorticoid dependence: option 1, assess the alternate-day prednisone threshold (below 15 mg/m2, 0.5 mg/kg; if remission, alternate-day prednisone 0.1 to below 0.5 mg/kg/dose; with glucocorticoid toxicity go to option 2; if no remission go to option 2); option 2, start a second-line agent if previous long-term glucocorticoid use with signs of toxicity. Glucocorticoid resistance: kidney biopsy, then therapy based on histological diagnosis.

text:
**Flowchart: Treatment algorithm for NS in a newly nephrotic child**

Diagram: Treatment algorithm for NS in a newly nephrotic child (section: Pharmacological Management of Glomerulonephritis)
- New Nephrotic -> ≥12 years of age Syndromic features or family history; ≤12 years of age No syndromic features or family history
- ≥12 years of age Syndromic features or family history -> Glucocorticoids*
- ≤12 years of age No syndromic features or family history -> Biopsy and/or genetic testing + referral to specialty center
- Glucocorticoids* -> No response x 4 or 6 weeks; Complete responder
- No response x 4 or 6 weeks -> Genetic testing • Kidney biopsy • Calcineurin inhibitor • Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system blockade
- Complete responder -> Glucocorticoids* X 8 or 12 weeks
- Glucocorticoids* X 8 or 12 weeks -> Frequent relapser; Infrequent relapser; Steroid-dependent
- Frequent relapser -> Cyclophosphamide • Levamisole • Mycophenolate mofetil • Rituximab • Calcineurin inhibitor
- Infrequent relapser -> Glucocorticoids*
- Steroid-dependent -> Mycophenolate mofetil • Rituximab • Calcineurin inhibitor • Cyclophosphamide

Treatment algorithm for a newly nephrotic child (NCDIMH guidelines, page 228). Aged 12 years or younger without syndromic features or family history: glucocorticoids. Aged over 12 years, or with syndromic features or family history: biopsy and/or genetic testing and referral to a specialty centre. On glucocorticoids, no response after 4 or 6 weeks: genetic testing, kidney biopsy, calcineurin inhibitor and renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system blockade. Complete responders: glucocorticoids for 8 or 12 weeks, then by relapse pattern. Frequent relapser: cyclophosphamide, levamisole, mycophenolate mofetil, rituximab or a calcineurin inhibitor. Infrequent relapser: glucocorticoids again. Steroid-dependent: mycophenolate mofetil, rituximab, calcineurin inhibitor or cyclophosphamide.

narrative: When to consider a kidney biopsy in patients with proteinuria and/or glomerular haematuria (NCDIMH guidelines, page 228). The kidney biopsy is the gold standard for glomerular disease; perform it if the result is expected to change treatment or more prognostic information is needed. Patients classically treated without biopsy: children aged 12 years or younger with steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome, and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. Treatment may also be considered without biopsy confirmation in: PLA2R antibody positive, PR3 ANCA vasculitis, anti-GBM disease, Alport disease, Fabry disease, familial focal segmental glomerulosclerosis with well-characterised mutations, systemic lupus erythematosus, and when biopsy is contraindicated.

Steroid Sensitive
Initial: \*\*A\*\*: prednisolone 60mg/m2/d) or 2mg/kg/d \[max 60mg/d] for 6 weeks \[complete 6weeks of initial treatment if remission is attained at 4weeks) Continue:
\*\*A\*\*: prednisolone 40mg/m2 or 1.5mg/kg for 6weeks, if the patient has attained remission by 4weeks of initial treatment, after 6weeks of alternate days' therapy taper and stop within 6weeks (taper by 5-10mg a week)
Relapsing Steroid Sensitive 0.9% sodium chloride
\*\*A\*\*: prednisolone 60mg/m2 or 2mg/kg \[max 60mg/d] until in complete remission for 3 days, THEN
\*\*A\*\*: prednisolone single dose on alternate days (40mg/m2 per dose or 1.5mg/kg per dose: maximum 40 mg on alternate days) for at least 4 weeks.
\*\*S\*\*: levamisole (PO) 2.5mg/kg on alternate days for 12months
Frequent relapse steroid dependent S: cyclophosphamide 2mg/kg/d 10-12 weeks
\[max 168mg/kg cumulative dose] \*\*OR S\*\*: cyclosporine 4-5mg/kg/d (starting dose) OR S: tacrolimus 0.1mg/kg/d (starting dose) \*\*OR S\*\*: everolimus
0.5-2mg 12hourly OR S: sirolimus 1- 3mg 12hourly \*\*OR\*\*
\*\*S\*\*: mycophenolate mofetil 1200mg/m2/d in two divided doses | In children biopsy is indicated for
1. Children with steroid resistant NS
2. Late failure to respond following initial response
3. Decreasing kidney function
Monitor calcineurin inhibitor toxicity/ levels |

heading_path: Chapter 8: Neurology > Diagnosis of Epilepsy > Epilepsy Algorithm of Assessment and Management
text:
## **Epilepsy Algorithm of Assessment and Management**

| **1** | Person presents with episodes of convulsions (fits, shaking, stiffening) — witnessed or reported |
| --- | --- |
| **2** | Confirm 2+ unprovoked seizures (not febrile, not substance-related, not syncope). Onset, duration, frequency? |
| **3** | Rule out other causes: hypoglycaemia, head injury, meningitis, stroke, eclampsia, substance withdrawal |
| **4** | Assess: Postictal confusion? Tongue-biting? Urinary incontinence? Aura? Birth trauma history? |
| **5** | Check current medications; assess for pregnancy in women of childbearing age |
| **6** | Assess functional impairment: school, work, driving, daily activities, social life |
| **7** | Screen for mental health comorbidities (depression, anxiety) |
| **8** | DIAGNOSIS: Epilepsy confirmed — Proceed to management |

| **2** | Confirm 2+ unprovoked seizures (not febrile, not substance-related, not syncope). Onset, duration, frequency? |
| **3** | Rule out other causes: hypoglycaemia, head injury, meningitis, stroke, eclampsia, substance withdrawal |
| **4** | Assess: Postictal confusion? Tongue-biting? Urinary incontinence? Aura? Birth trauma history? |
| **5** | Check current medications; assess for pregnancy in women of childbearing age |
| **6** | Assess functional impairment: school, work, driving, daily activities, social life |
| **7** | Screen for mental health comorbidities (depression, anxiety) |
| **8** | DIAGNOSIS: Epilepsy confirmed — Proceed to management |

text:
### **EPILEPSY MANAGEMENT — PHARMACOLOGICAL TREATMENT**

**Antiepileptic Medications (AEMs): Start one medication at lowest dose; increase slowly until seizures controlled.**

1.  **Start low and go slow:** start with a single AED as monotherapy after deciding on the type of seizure (s) and epilepsy syndrome. Titrate the dose gradually according to the symptoms until reach the maximal dosage.
2.  If the first AED continues to be ineffective at the maximum tolerated dose, introduce an alternative AED slowly without tapering the first.
3.  If the patient has a good response to the second AED, consider withdrawing the original AED gradually.
4.  If the first add-on AED is ineffective, or produces undesirable side effects, withdraw it slowly, and simultaneously replace it with a second add-on AED from the remaining choices. This process can be repeated for other possible add-on AEDs.

5. If the seizures are still not adequately controlled on two AEDs, some patients may benefit from an additional third AED.
6. AED from a different mode of action is preferred for add-on therapy to possibly increase the chance of seizure control but importantly to avoid added side effects by using the AED of similar mode of action.
7. Review the diagnosis if seizures continue despite the above logical approach, and a period of 2-3 years has elapsed.

| Yes | **Start Third Line Therapy** / 1. Ketamine: 1-2mg/kg - bogus and 1-2mg/kg/hr continuous infusion for minimum of 24hr. / 2. Propofol: 1-3 mg/kg-bolus and 5-10mg/kg/hr. continuous infusion for 24hr / 3. Thiopental: 3-5 mg/kg-bolus and 3-3mg/kg/hr. continuous infusion for 24hr |
| Time | 5-15 minutes = first line therapy phase |
| Time | 15-30 minutes on ward = second line |
| Time | 30 minutes on ward = third line therapy phase |

text:
## **Cervical Cancer Screening & Management Summary Table**

| Component | General Population (HIV-Negative Women) | Women Living with HIV |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Start Age | 25 years | 25 years or at HIV diagnosis (whichever first) |
| Stop Age | After 50 years with 2 consecutive negative screens | After 50 years with 2 consecutive negative screens |
| Preferred Test | HPV DNA testing | HPV DNA testing |
| HPV Screening Interval (if negative) | Every 5 years | Every 3 years |
| If HPV Positive | Triage (VIA / colposcopy / cytology) | Triage (VIA / colposcopy / cytology) |
| Alternative Method (if HPV unavailable) | VIA | VIA ± VILI |
| VIA/VILI Interval | Every 2 years | Annually (every year) |
| Screening Approach | Screen-and-treat | Screen-and-treat integrated into HIV care |
| If VIA/VILI Negative | Rescreen at interval | Rescreen at interval |
| If VIA/VILI Positive & eligible | Same-day cryotherapy/thermal ablation | Same-day cryotherapy/thermal ablation |
| If not eligible for ablation | Refer for LEEP/colposcopy | Refer for LEEP/colposcopy/ oncology |
| Service Delivery Model | Primary care, MCH/OPD clinics | Routine HIV clinic visits (provider-initiated) |

text:
## **Risk Stratification for Breast Cancer**

| Risk Level | Criteria |
| --- | --- |
| **Above Average Risk** | - No family history- One first-degree relative or 1–2 second-degree relatives diagnosed at age 50 or older |
| **Moderately Increased Risk** | - A first-degree relative diagnosed **before** age 50- Two or more first-degree relatives on the same side of the family diagnosed at any age |
| **High Risk** | - Known to carry a breast cancer susceptibility gene mutation (e.g., **BRCA1** or **BRCA2**) |
|  | - Strong family history with at least **two first-degree relatives affected**, plus other features |

#### **By Looking**

Stand before a mirror and look at both breasts and nipples

**Once with both arms beside your body**

**Once with both hands on your hips**

**Once with both arms raised and arms behind your head**

#### **By Touching**

Raise your left arm. Use the pads of your 3 or 4 fingers of the right hand to examine your left breast. Repeat on the right side

**Once in lines up and down your breast from outside and inside**

**Once in circles around the breast making smaller circles towards the nipples**

**Once in wedges starting from outside towards nipples and back again**

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Breast Cancer > While Lying Down
text:
#### **While Lying Down**

Lie on your back, left arm over your head and a pillow under your left shoulder. Examine your left breast with your right hand as described before. Repeat for the right side. This position flattens the breast and makes it easier to examine.

#### **Lymph Nodes**

Place your left hand on your waist. With your right hand try to find enlarged lymph nodes in the left underarm area and around your collar bone. Repeat on your right side.

**An enlarged lymph node feels like a corn kernel or a bean**

At the primary clinic (for example general practitioner or school nurse), identify suspected cancer using the SILUAN signs (significant, unexplained, rapid onset, ongoing symptoms, night sweats). ### **Adjuvant diagnostic techniques**

1. Oral cytology
2. Salivary biomarkers
3. Light based techniques (auto-fluorescence, spectroscopy, chemiluminescence
4. Tissue staining

### **Diagnostic Workup**

If there is any suspicion of a lesion that may represent oral cavity cancer, the lesion site and size should be documented, a clinical photograph taken if possible, and urgent referral made to an Oral & Maxillofacial Surgeon who is involved in a Head and Neck Oncology MDT

Diagram: Clinical workflow for cataract diagnosis and management (section: Screening and Diagnosis of Cataract)
- Patient presents with visual complaints - Gradual, painless vision loss - Glare, haloes, blurred vision -> Clinical Assessment - Visual acuity - Lens exam (cloudiness) - Red reflex
- Clinical Assessment - Visual acuity - Lens exam (cloudiness) - Red reflex -> Rule out other causes of vision loss - Retinal disease - Glaucoma - Refractive errors
- Rule out other causes of vision loss - Retinal disease - Glaucoma - Refractive errors -> Confirm cataract diagnosis
- Confirm cataract diagnosis -> Assess impact on daily life - Daily activities - Bilateral/unilateral - Uncorrectable with glasses
- Assess impact on daily life - Daily activities - Bilateral/unilateral - Uncorrectable with glasses -> Refer to ophthalmologist - Full evaluation - Biometry
- Refer to ophthalmologist - Full evaluation - Biometry -> (Mild/early) Management: Early cataract - Monitor - Improve lighting - Adjust glasses; (Affects daily life) Management: Significant cataract - Surgery (Phacoemulsification + IOL)
- Management: Significant cataract - Surgery (Phacoemulsification + IOL) -> Post-operative Care - Eye drops - Follow-up - Patient education

narrative: Cataract diagnosis and management workflow (NCDIMH guidelines, page 278). A patient presents with gradual painless vision loss, glare, haloes or blurred vision. Clinical assessment: visual acuity, lens examination for cloudiness, red reflex. Rule out other causes of vision loss (retinal disease, glaucoma, refractive errors). Confirm cataract, then assess the impact on daily life (daily activities, bilateral or unilateral, not correctable with glasses). Refer to an ophthalmologist for full evaluation and biometry. Mild or early cataract: monitor, improve lighting, adjust glasses. Cataract affecting daily life: surgery (phacoemulsification with intraocular lens), then post-operative care with eye drops, follow-up and patient education.

text:
**REFER ALL SEVERE/SIGNIFICANT CATARACT CASES TO EYE SURGEON FOR CATARACT SURGERY.**
**Refer all clients with other comorbidities such as HTN/DM as well as pregnant women with cataract once a**
**year to Ophthalmologist from diagnosis for annual routine screening.**

**Children should be referred immediately, a white pupil in children may be a tumor in the eye and late referral**
**may lead to permanent loss of vision, squint, loss of eye or loss of life.**

heading_path: Chapter 10: Ophthalmology > Diabetic Retinopathy (DR) > Definition and Classification of Diabetic Retinopathy (DR) > Classification of DR
text:
## **Classification of DR**

Can be classified as follows:
| **DR Severity** | **Defining Features** | **Management** | **Follow-up** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| No Dr | No microvascular abnormalities | Control blood levels, serum lipid levels, and blood pressure | 1-2 yrs |
| Mild NPDR | Microaneurysms only | Control blood glucose levels, serum lipid levels, and blood pressure | 6-12mo |
| Moderate NPDR | Microaneurysms and other signs (dot and blot hermorrhages, hard exudates, cotton wool spots), but not severe NPDR | Control blood glucose levels, serum lipid levels, and blood pressure | 3-6 mo |
| Severe NPDR | Intraretinal hemorrhages (>20 in each of 4 quadrants), definite venous beading (in at least 2 quadrants), or apparent IRMA (in at least 1 quadrant), but not PDR | Consider PRP | <3 mo |
| PDR | Neovascularization of optic disc or elsewhere, preretinal hemorrhage, or vitreous hemorrhage | Strong consider PRP, consider vitrectomy for persistent vitreous hemorrhage or tractional retinal detachment | <1 mo (variable) |
| DME | Retinal thickening in the macula | Consider focal laser photocoagulation, anti-VEGF therapy, or corticosteroid therapy for center-involving DME | 1-3 mo |

## Diagnosis

#### **Signs and Symptoms**

No symptoms in early stages of the disease, as the disease progresses the following might develop:
* Fluctuating vision
* Blurred vision
* Spots or floaters
* Dark or empty areas in vision
* Total loss of vision

narrative: Screening and diagnosis of diabetic retinopathy (NCDIMH guidelines, page 281). Start by collecting the diabetes history, medical history, current medication and biochemical parameters. Then do two assessments: measure uncorrected visual acuity (VA) with the client's current spectacles, and perform ophthalmoscopy or fundus photography. If VA is better than 6/12 (20/40), do routine re-examination. If VA is 6/12 (20/40) or worse, make a non-urgent referral for refraction and assessment. On ophthalmoscopy or fundus photography, if there is no retinopathy, do routine re-examination; if there is mild or moderate non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR), make a non-urgent referral for refraction and assessment; if there is severe NPDR, diabetic macular edema (DME) or proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR), make an urgent referral.

heading_path: Chapter 11: Palliation > Pain Management > Category of Drugs
text:
### **Category of Drugs**

**Non-opioids** Ibuprofen or other NSAID, paracetamol (acetaminophen), or aspirin
**Weak opioids** Codeine, tramadol, or low-dose morphine
**Strong opioids** Morphine, Fentanyl, Oxycodone, Hydromorphone, Buprenorphine
**Adjuvants** Antidepressant, Anticonvulsant, Antispasmodic, Muscle relaxant, Bisphosphonate, or Corticosteroid.
* Combining an opioid and non-opioid is effective, but do not combine drugs of the same class.
* Time doses based on drug half-life (“dose by the clock”); do not wait for pain to recur.

# Health Center/ Primary Care Clinic

- Holistic pain assessment
- Pain and symptoms management using the WHO pain management Ladder.
- Provide emotional support.
- Liaise with CHWs who visit patients at home with palliative care needs.
- Request for oral morphine solution for PC patient under HC catchment area
- Request advice from regional hospital if needed
- Refer to the regional level hospital for complicated cases.

#### **Classification**

| **Ulcer** **Grade** | **Description** | **Category** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **0** | No ulcer but high-risk foot (e.g., deformity, callus, or ischemia) | Non-ulcer stage |
| **1** | Superficial ulcer involving only the skin | Non-gangrenous ulcer |
| **2** | Deep ulcer, extending into tendon, bone, or joint capsule, but without bony involvement or abscess | Non-gangrenous ulcer |
| **3** | Deep ulcer with abscess, osteomyelitis, or joint sepsis (confirmed clinically or by X-ray) | Non-gangrenous ulcer |
| **4** | Localized gangrene (e.g., toe, heel, forefoot) | Gangrenous ulcer |
| **5** | Extensive gangrene involving the whole foot | Gangrenous ulcer |

heading_path: Chapter 12: Podiatry > Diabetic Foot > Tuning Fork Examination
text:
## **Tuning Fork Examination** | **How to perform Tuning Fork Test** | | | --- | --- | | | 1. Ask patient to close his/her eyes.
2. Tap a 128 Hz tuning fork and place it on patient’s sternum to confirm vibration.
3. Tap tuning fork and place it on bony prominence of the foot (distal phalanx of the great toe).
4. Ask patient to tell you when vibration is felt on the foot and tell you when it stops.
5. If sensation is impaired, continue to assess more proximally (e.g. mid-dorsal foot, medial malleolus, midfibular, patella)
6. Repeat assessment on the other leg.

**Note:** Any bony prominence of the foot can be tested. However, the best point for vibration test is at the great toe. |

### **Off-Loading Techniques for DFUs** | | | | | | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Technique
Total Contact Cast (TCC)
Removable Cast Walkers (RCWs) / Braces | Description
Cast that encompasses foot & ankle, redistributing pressure
Custom-fitted, removable devices for off-loading | Indications
Moderate–severe plantar DFUs; no infection or significant ischemia
Mild–moderate DFUs, or if TCC not feasible | Advantages
• Gold standard for off-loading • Promotes wound healing • Reduces recurrence & re- ulceration
• Allows wound inspection & hygiene • More comfortable & easier to use | Disadvantages
• Hard to monitor wound • Skin maceration risk • Fall/ambulation difficulty
• Less effective than TCC • Compliance issues if removed too often | Care Considerations
• Keep dry & intact • Weekly reviews for skin breakdown or infection
• Use with proper footwear • Patient education on strict off-loading | | Cushioned Footwear | Shoes with cushioned insoles, rocker soles, or extra depth | Mild DFUs, patients needing frequent ambulation | • Comfortable & non-invasive • Redistributes pressure, especially when combined with other techniques | • Not effective for moderate–severe ulcers • Requires consistent use | • Regular podiatry inspection & fitting |

narrative: Treatment of neuropathic pain in the diabetic foot (NCDIMH guidelines, page 305). For a patient with painful neuropathy, rule out other causes, establish treatment goals and optimise glycaemic control. First-line: anticonvulsants (pregabalin, gabapentin) or antidepressants (tricyclics and SNRIs: amitriptyline, duloxetine). Second-line: SNRIs (venlafaxine or desvenlafaxine), opioid-like drugs (tramadol or tapentadol extended release) or topical treatments (lidocaine 5% patch or capsaicin 0.075% cream). Third-line: SSRIs (citalopram or paroxetine) or opioids (controlled-release oxycodone; escitalopram is also listed).

heading_path: Chapter 13: Pyschiatry > Depression Management-Pharmacological Treatment
text:
| **Cautions & Special Populations** |
| --- |
| If manic episode occurs: STOP antidepressant immediately (may be bipolar disorder) |
| Do not combine antidepressants — risk of serotonin syndrome |
| SSRIs may increase suicidal ideation in adolescents/young adults — weekly monitoring for first 4 weeks |
| Pregnancy: avoid if possible; if severe, use lowest effective dose with specialist input |
| Breastfeeding: fluoxetine and sertraline generally considered safer options |
| Elderly: start low, go slow; monitor for falls, hyponatraemia (SSRIs) |
| Epilepsy co-morbidity: avoid tricyclics (lower seizure threshold) |

heading_path: Chapter 13: Pyschiatry > Depression Management-Pharmacological Treatment
text:
| **SUICIDE RISK ASSESSMENT — Mandatory in all depression cases** |  |
| --- | --- |
| Ask directly: ‘Are you having thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life?’ |  |
| If YES: Assess — Plan? Method? Intent? Previous attempts? Access to means (medications, weapons)? |  |
| HIGH RISK: Hospitalize / urgent referral; remove access to lethal means immediately |  |
| MEDIUM RISK: Safety plan, close follow-up within 2-3 days, involve trusted person/carer |  |
| ALL risk levels: do not leave alone; mobilize social support; document safety plan |  |

| **FOLLOW-UP — Depression (2 weeks initially, then monthly, then every 3 months)** |  |
| --- | --- |
| Weeks 2-4: Assess for side effects, suicidal ideation (especially adolescents on SSRIs) |  |
| Week 4-6: Has mood/interest improved? If no response — increase dose or switch medication |  |
| Week 8-12: Full remission expected; reinforce adherence for full treatment course (9-12 months minimum) |  |
| After 9-12 months symptom-free: discuss gradual tapering with patient — taper over weeks to months |  |
| 3+ recurrent episodes: consider long-term maintenance therapy to prevent relapse |  |
| Screen for re-emergence of symptoms at every follow-up visit after stopping treatment |  |

heading_path: Chapter 13: Pyschiatry > Suicide > Warning Signs of Suicidal Behaviour
text:
## **Warning Signs of Suicidal Behaviour** Suicidal behaviour emerges from a diverse range of factors, spanning individuals, interpersonal, communal and societal.
  • Feeling like a burden
  • Being isolated
  • Increased anxiety
  • Talking about feeling trapped or in unbearable pain
  • Increased substance use
  • Looking for a way to access lethal means
  • Increased anger or rage
  • Extreme mood swings
  • Expressing hopelessness and having no reason to live
  • Sleeping too little or too much
  • Talking or posting about wanting to die or to kill self
  • Making plans for suicide
  • Giving away prized possessions
  • Showing rage or talking about seeking revenge
  • Suddenly, coming out from being hopeless
  • Not wanting to complete projects, one has started
    • | Warning signs to look out for | | | --- | --- | | | |

heading_path: Chapter 14: Pulmonology > Bronchial Asthma > Diagnostic Tests for Bronchial Asthma
text:
### **Key Diagnostic Criteria**

Diagnosis requires history of variable respiratory symptoms AND variable expiratory airflow limitation:
* Symptoms: wheezing, shortness of breath, chest tightness, cough
* Symptoms vary over time and in intensity; worsen at night/early morning
* Symptoms triggered by: exercise, allergens, cold air, irritants, viral infections
* Confirmed variable airflow limitation (spirometry preferred for ≥ 6 yrs)

Viral Respiratory Infections

| Inhaled Foreign Body | Sudden onset cough, unilateral wheeze, localized decreased breath sounds |
| Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) | Cough worse when lying down, heartburn, sour taste in mouth |
| Obliterative Bronchiolitis | Progressive dyspnea, fixed airflow obstruction, history of toxic exposure |
| Large Airway Stenosis | Biphasic stridor, difficulty breathing, fixed airway obstruction |
| Lung Cancer | Persistent cough, weight loss, hemoptysis, smoking history |
| Sarcoidosis | Hilar lymphadenopathy, dry cough, skin lesions, uveitis |

heading_path: Chapter 14: Pulmonology > Asthma Severity & Control Assessment
text:
### **Asthma Severity & Control Assessment**

GINA 2024 bases severity on the treatment step required to achieve good control. Assess symptom control at every visit To initiate treatment, the level of control must be assessed, focusing on two domains: **Symptom control** and **future risk** of adverse outcomes. Both domains should always be assessed.

* If the child’s asthma is **partly or well controlled**, they can be placed in Step 1 or Step 2 of treatment, provided there is no other serious risk for future exacerbation.
* If the child’s asthma is **uncontrolled**, they will be placed in Step 3–5 of treatment.

text:
## **Severity Classification (Retrospective – Based on Minimum Step for Control)**

> **GINA 2024 Key Change: Preferred Reliever is Now Low-Dose ICS-Formoterol (AIR Strategy)**
>
SABA-only as reliever is no longer the preferred option for any step in adolescents and adults.
Anti-Inflammatory Reliever (AIR) = as-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol (e.g. budesonide-formoterol 200/6 mcg).
This strategy reduces exacerbations by ≥ 60% compared with SABA alone.

heading_path: Chapter 14: Pulmonology > Asthma Severity & Control Assessment > ICS Dose Ranges – Children 6-11 Years
text:
## **3 KEY POINTS FOR 6–11 YEAR AGE GROUP** Confirm diagnosis with **spirometry (FEV1/FVC < 0.80 abnormal in children)**

* Preferred inhaler device: MDI + spacer for all ages; DPI suitable from ~7 yrs with good technique
* ICS-LABA approved from age 6 years; use fixed-dose combination where available
* LABA should never be used without ICS in children
* LTRA (montelukast) is an alternative/add-on especially in allergic rhinitis co-morbidity; note FDA black box warning for neuropsychiatric events
* Tiotropium (LAMA) mist inhaler is licensed as add-on from age 6 years (Step 4–5)

#### **Important Note: Under-5 Asthma Management**

heading_path: Chapter 14: Pulmonology > Asthma Severity & Control Assessment > Additional Under-5 Considerations
text:
## **Additional Under-5 Considerations**

* LABA are NOT recommended as a drug class in children under 5 years
* LAMAs are not approved in this age group
* Allergen immunotherapy: not routinely recommended < 5 years
* Montelukast (LTRA): 4 mg granules/chewable for 2–5 yrs; may help in allergic or exercise-induced symptoms but evidence weaker than ICS
* Intermittent high-dose ICS during viral triggers (episodic ICS): may be considered in pure viral-triggered wheeze as an alternative to daily ICS at Steps 1–2
* Monitor height and weight at every visit – systemic ICS effects are a concern with high doses

heading_path: Chapter 14: Pulmonology > Management of Acute Asthma Exacerbations > Non-Pharmacological Interventions
text:
### **Non-Pharmacological Interventions**

| **Intervention** | **Key Points** |
| --- | --- |
| **Trigger avoidance** | Identify and reduce allergens, tobacco smoke, NSAIDs/aspirin (if sensitive), occupational irritants |
| **Inhaler education** | Check and correct technique at EVERY visit; MDI+spacer equivalent to nebuliser for most indications |
| **Written Asthma Action Plan** | Provide to all patients; include when to increase treatment, when to seek emergency care |
| **Physical activity** | Encourage regular exercise; warm-up reduces EIB; use pre-exercise SABA or ICS-LABA if needed |
| **Breathing exercises** | Buteyko, yoga breathing; evidence for symptom improvement though not lung function |
| **Weight reduction** | Obesity worsens asthma control; weight loss improves FEV1, symptoms, and quality of life |
| **Allergen immunotherapy** | SCIT or SLIT for allergic asthma (≥ 5 yrs); reduces exacerbations and ICS requirement |

heading_path: Chapter 14: Pulmonology > Management of Acute Asthma Exacerbations > All Age Groups – Immediate Actions
text:
### **All Age Groups – Immediate Actions:**

* Oxygen to achieve SpO2 94–98% (adults/adolescents) or 94–98% (children)
* SABA: salbutamol 4–10 puffs via MDI + spacer every 20 min × 3 (first hour)
* For severe: nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg (children) / 5 mg (adults) every 20 min
* Ipratropium bromide: add 0.5 mg (adults) / 0.25 mg (children) to nebuliser for moderate–severe
* Systemic corticosteroids: prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day (max 40 mg, children) OR 40–50mg/day (adults) × 5–7 days
* IV magnesium sulfate: 2g IV over 20 min (adults/adolescents) or 25–75mg/kg (children) for severe, SpO2 < 92%

* Severe or life-threatening features present
* SpO2 < 92% after initial treatment
* No improvement after 1 hour of treatment
* PEF remains < 40% after initial treatment
* Unable to maintain oral intake (children)
* Concern about home environment / adherence

narrative: Management of acute asthma exacerbations in primary care (NCDIMH guidelines, page 338). Assess the patient: is it asthma, are there risk factors for asthma-related death, how severe is the exacerbation? Mild or moderate: talks in phrases, prefers sitting, not agitated, pulse 100-120 per minute, oxygen saturation 90-95% on air, peak expiratory flow (PEF) 50% of predicted or best. Severe: talks in words, sits hunched, agitated, respiratory rate above 30 per minute, pulse above 120, saturation below 90%, PEF below 50%. Life-threatening: drowsy, confused, silent chest. Mild or moderate or severe: start treatment with a short-acting beta agonist (SABA) 4-10 puffs by pMDI and spacer, repeated every 20 minutes for 1 hour, prednisolone (adults 40-50 mg; children 1-2 mg/kg, maximum 40 mg), and controlled oxygen if available (target 93-95%; children 94-98%). If worsening, or severe or life-threatening, transfer to an acute care facility, giving SABA, ipratropium bromide, oxygen and systemic corticosteroids while waiting. If improving, continue SABA as needed and reassess at 1 hour. Discharge if symptoms improved without SABA, PEF improving above 60-80% of best, saturation above 94% on room air, and adequate resources at home. Follow up: review whether the exacerbation is resolving, whether to continue prednisolone, reduce the reliever, continue the controller (short term 1-2 weeks or long term 3 months), and correct risk factors including inhaler technique and adherence; refer if more than 1-2 exacerbations.

narrative: Management of acute asthma exacerbations in adults, adolescents and children 6-11 years (NCDIMH guidelines, page 339). Initial assessment of airway, breathing and circulation. If drowsiness, confusion or silent chest: consult ICU, start short-acting beta agonist (SABA) and oxygen, and prepare for intubation. Otherwise triage by the worst clinical feature. Mild or moderate: talks in phrases, prefers sitting, not agitated, pulse printed as 100-200 per minute (likely 100-120), saturation 90-95% on air, peak expiratory flow (PEF) above 50% of predicted or best; give SABA, oxygen to keep saturation 94-98%, and oral corticosteroids. Severe: talks in words, sits hunched, agitated, respiratory rate above 30, accessory muscles, pulse above 120, saturation below 90%, PEF below 50%; give SABA, ipratropium bromide, oxygen to saturation 94-98%, oral or IV corticosteroids, consider IV magnesium sulfate and IV terbutaline or aminophylline. If deterioration continues, treat as severe and reassess for ICU, transferring if necessary. One hour after initial treatment, measure lung function in all patients: FEV1 or PEF 60-80% of predicted or personal best with improved symptoms is moderate, consider discharge; below 60% or no clinical response is severe, continue treatment and reassess frequently.

text:
**IV salbutamol can be used in patients with severe asthma who fail to respond to other treatments, mainly to prevent intubation.**  
**In patients with severe attacks, there is very limited evidence that IV beta 2-agonists reduce recovery time or improve pulmonary function.**

The rationale to support IV salbutamol is that inhaled drugs may have a limited effect in patients with nearly complete airway obstruction and have practical limitations in ventilated patients.  
Cardiac responses, such as arrhythmia and tachycardia, increased lactate and anxiety are significant side effects, which may increase respiratory workload and exacerbate respiratory failure.

Patients receiving IV salbutamol should be in a ICU setting.

---

**Most guidelines do not recommend use of IV aminophylline because of its low efficacy and safety profiles.**  
It improves diaphragmatic contractility.

If used, this bronchodilator should be reserved solely for clients with a **severe asthma exacerbation**, who have failed to improve despite maximal therapy (continuous inhaled beta 2-agonists, IV corticosteroids, IV magnesium sulfate) and generally in a high care/ICU setting.

The risk-benefit balance of IV aminophylline is unfavorable.

---

text:
### **Spirometry**

Spirometry is the gold standard for the diagnosis, assessment, and management of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary. It assesses the degree of airflow limitation. A post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio below 0.7 confirms persistent airflow limitation, suggesting COPD when accompanied by relevant symptoms. Additionally, an FEV1 value less than 80% of the predicted value indicates the severity of the airflow obstruction. The FEV1/FVC ratio is a sensitive marker for COPD detection. It’s essential to measure these values after administering a bronchodilator to ensure accuracy in differentiating it from asthma and evaluating other respiratory conditions.

narrative: Step-wise pharmacological management of COPD (NCDIMH guidelines, page 344). Step 1: short-acting bronchodilator for breathlessness, either a beta-2 agonist (salbutamol 100-200 mcg, 1-2 puffs as needed) or an anticholinergic (ipratropium 20-40 mcg three to four times daily). If symptom control is poor, step 2: combine short-acting bronchodilators from different groups (salbutamol and ipratropium). If still poor, step 3: add a long-acting bronchodilator (for example salmeterol 50 mcg twice daily) with the short-acting ones. If still poor, step 4: combine a long-acting bronchodilator and an inhaled corticosteroid (for example beclomethasone 200 mcg), stopping the corticosteroid after 4 weeks if there is no benefit. If still poor, step 5: consider adding sustained-release theophylline 250-500 mg twice daily, monitoring plasma levels and interactions.

Step-wise pharmacological management of COPD (NCDIMH guidelines, page 344). Step 1: short-acting bronchodilator for breathlessness, either a beta-2 agonist (salbutamol 100-200 mcg, 1-2 puffs as needed) or an anticholinergic (ipratropium 20-40 mcg three to four times daily). If symptom control is poor, step 2: combine short-acting bronchodilators from different groups (salbutamol and ipratropium). If still poor, step 3: add a long-acting bronchodilator (for example salmeterol 50 mcg twice daily) with the short-acting ones. If still poor, step 4: combine a long-acting bronchodilator and an inhaled corticosteroid (for example beclomethasone 200 mcg), stopping the corticosteroid after 4 weeks if there is no benefit. If still poor, step 5: consider adding sustained-release theophylline 250-500 mg twice daily, monitoring plasma levels and interactions.
